nodes.label: Stakeholder & SME Interviewing
nodes.one_line: Pull the real task knowledge out of a sponsor or SME's head instead of the sanitized version they lead with.
know_what: Tacit knowledge — expert knowledge that's automatic enough the expert can't easily narrate it without a structured prompt
Critical incident technique — asking for a specific recent example ('walk me through the last time this went wrong') instead of a general description
Leading vs. open question — a question that supplies its own answer versus one that lets the interviewee surface what actually matters
Sponsor vs. SME vs. end-user — three different interview subjects with different blind spots and different stakes in the answer
Interview guide — a prepared but flexible question set that ensures coverage without turning the interview into a script read aloud
Saying-doing gap — the well-documented gap between how someone describes their process and what they actually do
know_how: Open with a critical-incident question ('tell me about the last time this happened') instead of an abstract one ('what's your process')
Follow a vague answer with 'what exactly did you do next' until the tacit steps surface
Interview the sponsor, at least one SME, and at least one end-user separately, since their answers will diverge
Observe the task being performed when possible, to catch the gap between the interview account and the actual behavior
Keep an interview guide as a checklist, not a script, and let follow-ups take priority over finishing the list
Write up notes within an hour of the interview, before the specific phrasing is lost
habits: Ask 'what exactly do you mean by that' whenever a term sounds like jargon everyone's supposed to already understand
Distrust any account that's suspiciously procedural and clean — real expertise has more exceptions than that
Let silence sit instead of filling it with a leading suggestion
Take the sponsor's opening framing as one data point, not the finding
Look for what an SME does that they didn't think to mention
nodes.checkpoint: Conduct and write up an interview with a subject-matter expert using critical-incident technique, producing notes that specify at least three concrete steps or decisions the expert didn't initially think to mention.
nodes.common_failure: Asking 'what's your process' and transcribing the tidy, after-the-fact narrative the expert gives, which omits the tacit judgment calls that actually make them an expert.
sources: John Flanagan, The Critical Incident Technique
Cathy Moore, Action Mapping interview approach
Beth Kanter & practitioner guidance on SME interviewing

nodes.label: Learner Audience Profiling
nodes.one_line: Describe who is actually going to take the course — prior knowledge, motivation, access — well enough to design for them instead of yourself.
know_what: Prior knowledge — what the audience already knows, the single biggest predictor of how much guidance a design needs
Motivation type — mandatory or compliance audiences versus self-selected audiences, which need different framing and pacing
Access constraints — device, bandwidth, language, and disability considerations that rule out design options before you propose them
Persona vs. profile — a persona is illustrative fiction; a profile is data (headcount, role mix, prior scores, survey results); don't mistake one for the other
Learner variance within a group — 'the audience' that's actually three different sub-audiences with different needs
Job context — where and when the learner will actually apply the skill (at a desk, on a floor, mid-call), which shapes format choices
know_how: Pull existing data (HR records, prior assessment scores, support tickets) before inventing a persona from assumption
Segment an apparently single audience into sub-groups when their prior knowledge or motivation clearly diverges
Check device and bandwidth constraints directly with IT or the field, not by assuming everyone has a laptop and broadband
Note where and when the learner will use the skill, and flag any design idea that assumes a context they don't have (quiet room, spare time)
State assumptions about the audience explicitly and mark which are data-backed and which are guesses
Revisit the profile when pilot data contradicts it, instead of treating the original profile as fixed
habits: Ask 'says who' about every audience claim that isn't backed by data
Picture a specific real person from the audience, not an averaged composite, when making a design call
Check for sub-groups before assuming the whole audience is one profile
Ask what the learner will be holding, wearing, or doing when they need this skill
Treat a persona as a summary of data already gathered, never as a substitute for gathering it

know_why.claim: A learner persona is a useful design tool.
know_why.because: a concrete, named persona makes design decisions faster and more consistent across a team than an abstract 'the learner'
know_why.disputed_by: data-first practitioners who argue personas invite designers to design for a comfortable fiction instead of the messier real data, and prefer working directly from segmented profile data
know_why.source: UX persona methodology (Alan Cooper) adapted into ID practice, vs. evidence-based L&D critiques (e.g. Will Thalheimer)

nodes.checkpoint: Given access to existing learner data, produce an audience profile with at least two sub-segments, each with prior knowledge, motivation, and access constraints stated separately, with every claim marked as data-backed or assumed.
nodes.common_failure: Writing a single generic audience profile ('busy adult professionals') that's vague enough to justify any design choice, instead of specific enough to rule any out.
sources: Will Thalheimer on learner personas and evidence

nodes.label: Task Analysis
nodes.one_line: Break a job task into the exact steps and decision points an expert makes without noticing.
know_what: Hierarchical task analysis (HTA) — breaking a task into a goal, sub-goals, and operations, shown as a tree
Cognitive task analysis (CTA) — extracting the decision points and judgment calls behind a task, not just the observable steps
Procedural vs. principled task — a task with one correct sequence versus one that depends on situational judgment
Decision point — a step in a task where an expert branches based on a condition a novice might not even notice exists
Task inventory — the full list of tasks a role performs, used to decide which ones actually need training versus a job aid
Step granularity — the level of detail a task breakdown needs, calibrated to how much a novice can already do without help
know_how: Build a hierarchical task analysis tree for a task, breaking it into sub-goals and then into discrete operations
Interview or observe an expert specifically to extract decision points, asking 'how did you know to do that instead of the other thing'
Classify each task in a task inventory as procedural (fixed sequence, good for a checklist or job aid) or principled (situational judgment, good for training)
Calibrate step granularity to the audience profile — more granular for true novices, coarser for an audience with related experience
Cross-check a task breakdown with a second expert to catch idiosyncratic steps that aren't actually standard
Flag any procedural task that's better solved with a job aid than with training time
habits: Ask 'how did you know' at every branch point instead of accepting a step as self-evident
Watch for the step an expert skips describing because it's become automatic for them
Separate 'this is how I do it' from 'this is the only correct way to do it'
Check whether a task belongs in training at all or would be cheaper as a job aid
Cross-check a surprising step with a second expert before trusting it's standard practice
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a hierarchical task analysis for a moderately complex job task, including at least two identified decision points that a novice wouldn't notice without the analysis.
nodes.common_failure: Writing a task analysis that's really just a numbered list of what the expert does, missing the decision points and conditions that make the task actually hard to learn.
sources: Jonassen, Tessmer & Hannum, Task Analysis Methods for Instructional Design
Crandall, Klein & Hoffman, Working Minds (cognitive task analysis)

nodes.label: Gap & Root-Cause Diagnosis
nodes.one_line: Sort a performance gap into its real cause — skill, knowledge, environment, or incentive — instead of defaulting to 'they need training.'
know_what: Behavior Engineering Model (Gilbert) — six factors (information, resources, incentives, skill, capacity, motives) sorted into environment vs. person
Skill/knowledge deficit — a gap caused by the person genuinely not knowing or being unable to do the thing
Environmental deficit — a gap caused by missing information, tools, or incentives in the environment, not the person
Motivation vs. capacity — whether someone won't do the behavior versus can't do it, which imply opposite fixes
Root-cause vs. symptom — the difference between the visible problem (missed deadlines) and its actual driver (an unclear handoff process)
Fishbone / 5 Whys — lightweight root-cause techniques for tracing a symptom back through contributing causes
know_how: Run a Behavior Engineering Model pass on a reported gap, checking all six factors before concluding it's a skill or knowledge issue
Apply 5 Whys to a stated problem to trace it back past the first, most obvious cause
Distinguish a 'won't' from a 'can't' by checking whether the person can perform the behavior under direct observation or incentive
Rule out environmental causes (missing job aid, broken process, absent incentive) before recommending training
Write the root-cause finding in a form that names the specific factor, not just 'training gap', so the fix matches the cause
Flag when a gap has multiple root causes and needs a combined intervention, not a single fix
habits: Ask 'is this a won't or a can't' before proposing any fix
Run through all six Gilbert factors even when the answer seems obvious after the first one
Resist stopping at the first plausible cause; ask why at least twice more
Notice when 'they need training' is really 'the process is broken' in disguise
Name the specific Gilbert factor in the finding instead of writing 'training gap' as a catch-all
nodes.checkpoint: Given a reported performance gap, apply the Behavior Engineering Model or 5 Whys to identify at least one environmental and one person-side contributing cause, with a fix recommendation matched to each.
nodes.common_failure: Diagnosing every gap as a skill deficit because that's the diagnosis that justifies building training, when the data actually points to a missing job aid or broken incentive.
sources: Thomas Gilbert, Human Competence (Behavior Engineering Model)
Robert Mager & Peter Pipe, Analyzing Performance Problems

nodes.label: Delivery Context & Constraints Mapping
nodes.one_line: Map the time, budget, technology, and regulatory limits that will rule out design options before you propose them.
know_what: Delivery constraint categories — time, budget, technology, regulatory or compliance, and organizational politics
Synchronous vs. asynchronous constraint — whether the audience can be gathered at one time, which rules out or requires live facilitation
Technology floor — the actual, verified minimum device and connectivity the audience has, not the IT department's assumed standard
Regulatory constraint — compliance requirements (accessibility law, industry certification rules) that are non-negotiable design inputs, not late-stage checks
Budget-to-scope ratio — the relationship between available budget and what level of production fidelity (text-only vs. custom video) is realistic
Political constraint — stakeholder relationships and organizational sensitivities that limit what content or framing is viable, regardless of instructional merit
know_how: Interview IT or field staff directly to verify the technology floor instead of assuming the documented standard is what people actually have
Convert a budget number into a realistic production fidelity level before promising a delivery format
Identify regulatory constraints (accessibility, certification) at the start of a project, not as a late compliance review
Map which stakeholders have veto power over content and note where that limits an otherwise sound design choice
Document constraints in writing and get sponsor sign-off, so a constraint discovered late doesn't get blamed on the designer
Distinguish a hard constraint that can't be changed from a soft preference that could be negotiated, before treating both as fixed
habits: Verify a stated constraint instead of taking a secondhand version of it at face value
Ask what happens if a constraint is violated, to test whether it's actually hard
Build the constraints list before the design proposal, not as a post-hoc excuse for scope cuts
Watch for a political constraint disguised as a technical or budget one
Get sponsor sign-off on the constraints list in writing before design starts
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a written constraints document for a project covering time, budget, technology, and regulatory limits, with each constraint marked as hard or negotiable and a named source for how it was verified.
nodes.common_failure: Discovering a hard constraint, such as a device limitation or an accessibility requirement, midway through production because it was assumed rather than verified at the start, forcing a costly redesign.
sources: Cathy Moore, Action Mapping scoping guidance

nodes.label: SME Collaboration Protocol
nodes.one_line: Run a review cycle with subject-matter experts that gets accurate sign-off without the scope creeping every round.
know_what: Review cycle — a defined number of SME review rounds, typically two to three, with a stated purpose for each, instead of open-ended back-and-forth
Scope boundary — a written statement of what's in and out of an SME's authority (content accuracy) versus the designer's (instructional method)
Turnaround SLA — an agreed time limit for SME feedback, without which reviews stall a project indefinitely
Change log — a record of what changed between review rounds and why, so a returning SME isn't re-litigating a settled decision
SME fatigue — the real, predictable drop in review quality and willingness after too many rounds, which argues for tight scoping over unlimited iteration
Escalation path — a named person to resolve an SME disagreement or a stalled review, agreed before the project starts
know_how: Set the number and purpose of review rounds (for example round 1 for content accuracy, round 2 for final polish) before the first draft goes out
Write a scope boundary into the kickoff agreement so an SME's late request to change the whole approach is easy to decline
Set and hold a turnaround SLA, escalating politely when a review stalls past it
Keep a change log visible to the SME so each round shows what was addressed since the last one
Batch minor content questions into a single check-in instead of pinging the SME for every small item
Name an escalation contact at kickoff for when an SME and the designer disagree on a content call
habits: Scope the review before the first draft, not after the first round of feedback arrives
Say no to a late-round request that's actually an earlier-round conversation, and name why
Track SME response time and flag a stalling reviewer early instead of waiting silently
Treat an SME's frustration with 'yet another round' as a scoping failure to fix, not a personality problem
Confirm the escalation contact by name before a disagreement actually happens, not after

know_why.claim: SME review should be capped at a fixed number of structured rounds, not left open-ended.
know_why.because: unlimited review rounds produce SME fatigue and diminishing returns, while a project with no defined end to review never actually finishes
know_why.disputed_by: SME-centric, expertise-heavy domains such as medical, legal, or safety-critical content, where practitioners argue accuracy risk justifies as many rounds as it takes, and a capped process trades safety for schedule
know_why.source: general ID project-management practice vs. regulated-industry (pharma, aviation, clinical) SME sign-off requirements

nodes.checkpoint: Run a two-round SME review on a real content draft, staying within an agreed turnaround SLA, with a change log documenting what was addressed each round and no scope creep into a design-method debate.
nodes.common_failure: Letting SME review become open-ended, where every round reopens decisions already made in an earlier round, until the review process consumes more time than the actual production.
sources: Cathy Moore, Action Mapping SME scoping
